newsitem.title: USA: Clinton choices reflect pressure for diversity.
newsitem.headline: Clinton choices reflect pressure for diversity.

text.p: WASHINGTON, Dec 20 (Reuter) President Clinton, who four years ago assembled a Cabinet that "looks like America" but downplayed such diversity this time, now has a dramatically changed team -- but one with a similar makeup.
Clinton on Friday announced the final members of the Cabinet-level group he wants in his second four-year term, which begins when he takes the oath of office Jan. 20.

The announcement ended an intense period of lobbying by various powerful groups that all tried to cash in the political chips they felt they had accumulated over the past four years and during the re-election campaign.

Clinton himself had stopped talking about wanting his Cabinet to reflect the face of America. When reporters asked him about the influences on him as he shaped his official team, he spoke of different goals this time around.

The politically born-again Clinton, who has been burying the liberal policies of his first years in the White House and striking the conservative-sounding goals of serving the "vital centre," said he would no longer set any kind of quotas in his selection process.
A person's qualifications was all that mattered, he told reporters, not the individual's sex or race or ethnic background, he said.
Shortly before Christmas four years ago Clinton's choices for Cabinet-level positions included four blacks, five women and two Hispanics.
At the same point this time around, even though many of the players have changed or been given different jobs, he has settled on a team that includes three blacks, five women and two Hispanics.
"I'm very proud of the first Cabinet that I appointed," Clinton told reporters at the end of his announcement ceremony. "I am very proud of this Cabinet."
"I am proud that they are diverse, but I would not have appointed a single one of them because of their gender or their racial or ethnic background had I not thought that they could succeed."
Clinton tried to downplay the pressures on him, but White House officials admit they were intense. The fight over who would follow Robert Reich as labour secretary serves as a good example.
The forces of organised labour rallied around former Sen. Harrison Wofford, a Pennsylvania Democrat who had by sympathic to union desires.
Black leaders pushed for Alexis Herman, one of their own who has been working at the White House.
Both groups have been potent forces in Democratic Party politics and not easy for Clinton to ignore.
Hoping to avoid angering either one, senior administration officials let it be known that Clinton was leaning toward Representative Esteban Torres, a California Democrat.

That, however, only fanned the flames rather than quelling them. Union officials and black leaders intensified their efforts, with civil rights leader Jessie Jackson making a personal appeal Thursday to Vice President Al Gore, who harbours his own interests in becoming president one day.
To the surprise of many, Clinton announced abruptly changed direction and announced he was picking Herman -- who also had the backing of women's groups.

Clinton, after taking the unusual step of publicly thanking both Wofford and Torres in announcing his selection of Herman, sought to downplay the forces that had been feverishly working to influence all his choices.
"The pressure was pressure I put on myself," he insisted in response to a reporter's question.

"I believe that one of my jobs at this moment in history is to demonstrate by the team I put together that no group of people should be excluded from service to our country ... So I have striven to achieve both excellence and diversity," he said.
